title: What cryptography is for
summary: Confidentiality, integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation: the four promises, and which tool keeps each.

steps.title: Four promises
body: Cryptography is a toolbox for keeping promises about data when you do **not** control where the data goes: across a network, onto a disk someone may steal, through a server you do not trust.
| Goal | The question it answers | Broken when |
| **Confidentiality** | Can only the intended people *read* it? | an eavesdropper learns the card number |
| **Integrity** | Has it been *changed*, even by one bit? | `amount=10` silently becomes `amount=1000` |
| **Authenticity** | Did it really come from *who it claims*? | a forged "reset your password" message |
| **Non-repudiation** | Can the sender later *deny* sending it? | "I never signed that contract" |
These are separate. Encryption alone gives confidentiality, but an attacker can often still flip bits in ciphertext and change what decrypts. You will see that happen in module 3.

steps.prompt: Match each failure to the promise it breaks.
pairs: A stolen laptop's database file is read by the thief
A proxy rewrites `to=alice` as `to=mallory` in transit
A webhook arrives claiming to be from your payment provider, but isn't
A customer says they never approved a signed order
steps.explain: Keep the four apart in your head: most real bugs come from getting one of them and assuming the others.

steps.title: One tool per promise
body: Each promise has a standard tool. You will build with every one of them in this topic.
| **Hash** (SHA-256) | none | a fingerprint: detects *accidental* change, but anyone can recompute it |
| **MAC** (HMAC-SHA256) | one shared secret | integrity + authenticity between people who share the key |
| **AEAD** (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) | one shared secret | confidentiality + integrity + authenticity in one call |
| **Signature** (ECDSA, RSA-PSS) | private key signs, public key verifies | integrity + authenticity + non-repudiation |
| **Key agreement** (ECDH) | key pairs | two strangers agree on a shared secret over a public channel |
Notice that a plain hash gives *no* authenticity: an attacker who changes the message just recomputes the hash.

steps.prompt: Which of these, used on its own, stops an attacker who can change the message *and* everything sent with it?
items: a SHA-256 hash sent next to the file
an HMAC-SHA256 tag with a key the attacker does not know
an ECDSA signature checked with a public key you already trust
steps.explain: Anything an attacker can recompute without a secret only catches accidents. A secret key (MAC, AEAD) or a private key (signature) is what makes forgery hard.

steps.prompt: Two microservices share a secret key and want to be sure messages between them were not forged. A later dispute *between the two services' owners* about who sent a message is not a concern. What is the simplest right tool?
options: An HMAC with the shared key
steps.explain: A MAC proves the message came from *someone holding the key*. With two parties that is enough. Non-repudiation needs a signature, because with a MAC either side could have produced the tag.

steps.title: What cryptography cannot do
body: Crypto moves the problem; it never removes it. Encrypting a database turns "protect the data" into "protect the **key**". Signing turns "trust the message" into "trust the **public key**", which is why certificates exist (see the *Certificates & PKI* topic).
It also cannot protect data while it is being used: a server that decrypts a record to show it is holding the plaintext in memory. And it cannot fix a bug in what you *do* with the decrypted data.
The rest of this topic is about using the tools correctly. Most failures you will meet are not broken algorithms, but correct algorithms used wrongly.

steps.prompt: A team encrypts every column of their database with AES and stores the key in `appsettings.json` in the same repository as the code. What have they mostly achieved?
options: Little: anyone who gets the code or the server gets the key too
Full protection, since AES is unbroken
steps.explain: Encryption is only as strong as the place the key lives. Module 5 is about where keys should live.

steps.prompt: A SHA-256 fingerprint is always the same size, whatever goes in. What does this print?
steps.explain: SHA-256 always outputs 256 bits, which is 32 bytes, for one byte or a million.

steps.title: Fingerprint a message
prompt: Write `string Fingerprint(string text)` that returns the SHA-256 hash of the text's UTF-8 bytes as **lowercase hex** (64 characters).

Then write `bool Unchanged(string text, string fingerprint)` that says whether the text still matches a fingerprint taken earlier. This catches accidental corruption; you will learn what stops a deliberate attacker in module 2.
template: Dojo.Eq("Fingerprint(\"\") is the hash of no bytes", "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855", Fingerprint(""));
Dojo.Eq("a fingerprint is 64 hex characters", 64, Fingerprint("a much longer message than three letters").Length);
Dojo.Check("the same text still matches", Unchanged("pay alice 10", dojoFp), "Unchanged returned false for the original text");
Dojo.Check("one changed character is caught", !Unchanged("pay alice 19", dojoFp), "Unchanged returned true for changed text");
hints: `SHA256.HashData(bytes)` hashes in one call; `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text)` gives you the bytes.
`Convert.ToHexStringLower(hash)` turns the 32 bytes into 64 lowercase hex characters.
